session.title: Quantifier order & witness dependence
session.focus: Nested quantifiers, scope and allowed dependence
session.purpose: Make nested quantifier order operational before later proof and analysis modules require parameter-dependent choices.
session.centralCapability: Read, construct, negate and refute two-quantifier claims while tracking which choices may depend on earlier quantified variables.
session.principalObstacle: Treating ∀x∃y and ∃y∀x as interchangeable, or using a witness chosen after x when the claim requires one witness chosen before x.
entryPrerequisites: M03-S05 universal/existential quantifiers over stated domains
M03-S06 exact negation of quantified claims
requiredOwnership: Read nested ∀∃ and ∃∀ claims in the stated order over explicit domains.
Explain when an existential witness may depend on an earlier universally quantified variable.
Distinguish input-dependent witnesses from one global witness that must work for every input.
Negate a two-quantifier claim by switching each quantifier, preserving domains and complementing the predicate.
Refute a false quantifier order with a legal adversarial choice made after the proposed global witness.
session.applicationScope: Elementary quantified claims over integers and finite assignment relations; no limit notation.
session.transferScope: Changed-surface Transfer: reconstruct dependence as a finite assignment/function problem rather than an inequality over integers.
outOfScope: epsilon-N or epsilon-delta definitions until M09
uniform convergence or advanced analysis terminology
choice axioms or infinite selection theorems
session.exitCondition: Solve the integer Main and finite-assignment Transfer while explicitly identifying who is chosen first, who may depend on whom, and why the reversed order succeeds or fails.
session.lesson: A quantified sentence is read in order. In ∀x∈X ∃y∈Y P(x,y), x is chosen first; after seeing that x, you may choose a y that can depend on x. A useful way to record this is y=f(x). In ∃y∈Y ∀x∈X P(x,y), y is chosen first, so the same y must survive every legal x; it may not be changed after x is revealed. To negate nested quantifiers, switch each quantifier and negate the final predicate while keeping the same domains: ¬(∀x∈X ∃y∈Y P(x,y)) is ∃x∈X ∀y∈Y ¬P(x,y), and ¬(∃y∈Y ∀x∈X P(x,y)) is ∀y∈Y ∃x∈X ¬P(x,y). Worked example: over integers, consider ∀n∈Z ∃k∈Z with k=n+2. It is true: once n is given, choose k=n+2. The reversed claim ∃k∈Z ∀n∈Z with k=n+2 is false: after a fixed k is proposed, choosing n=k makes the required equality k=k+2 impossible. The lesson is not that ∀∃ is always true or ∃∀ is always false; the predicate decides truth, while the quantifier order decides what dependence is allowed. Guided check: over real numbers, compare ∀x∈R ∃y∈R with y=3x−1 and ∃y∈R ∀x∈R with y=3x−1. For the first, write a witness rule. For the second, explain what a single y would have to do and give one x-choice that defeats a proposed y.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S31-M@1.prompt: Over the integers compare A: ∀n∈Z ∃m∈Z such that m>n and m−n is odd, with B: ∃m∈Z ∀n∈Z such that m>n and m−n is odd. For A, state the order of choice, give a witness rule m=m(n), and verify it. For B, state the order of choice and refute the claim by choosing a legal n after an arbitrary proposed m. Then write the exact logical negation of B, preserving the integer domains, and explain precisely why A permits dependence on n while B does not.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S31-T@1.prompt: Let X={a,b,c} and Y={1,2,3}. The allowed outputs are A(a)={1,2}, A(b)={2,3}, A(c)={1,3}. Decide whether (i) ∀x∈X ∃y∈Y with y∈A(x) and (ii) ∃y∈Y ∀x∈X with y∈A(x) are true. For (i), construct an explicit function f:X→Y whose value is allowed for every input and verify all three assignments. For (ii), either give one common y or prove that none exists by checking the candidates. Finish by explaining how this table represents input-dependent witnesses versus one global witness.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S31-M@1.reference: A is true: n is chosen first, then m=n+1 is an integer, m>n, and m−n=1 is odd. B is false: m would be fixed before n; for any proposed integer m choose n=m, making m>n false. The exact negation of B is ∀m∈Z ∃n∈Z such that ¬(m>n and m−n is odd), equivalently ∀m∈Z ∃n∈Z such that m≤n or m−n is even. A allows m to depend on n because ∃m occurs after ∀n; B requires one m before all n.

rubric.criterion: Reads A in the correct order: n is arbitrary first and the existential m may then be chosen as a function of n.
Uses a legal witness such as m=n+1 and verifies m∈Z, m>n and the odd difference.
Reads B in the correct order and refutes every proposed global m by a legal later choice such as n=m.
Writes the exact negation ∀m∈Z ∃n∈Z ¬(m>n and m−n is odd), or a logically equivalent form with the same domains.
Explains that A permits m to depend on n because the existential choice comes later, whereas B requires one fixed m to work for every n.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S31-M@1.marking: Accept any equivalent witness/refutation and any logically equivalent exact negation. Do not require the reference wording. A response that merely swaps symbols or states truth values without the dependence argument does not earn the corresponding credit.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S31-T@1.reference: (i) is true, for example f(a)=1,f(b)=2,f(c)=3; each value lies in Y and in the corresponding allowed set. (ii) is false because A(a)∩A(b)∩A(c)=∅: y=1 fails at b, y=2 fails at c, and y=3 fails at a. The function f records a witness chosen after x; (ii) asks for one y chosen before x and common to all three allowed sets.

rubric.criterion: Correctly decides that the ∀x∃y statement is true and supplies an explicit function f:X→Y.
Verifies all three assigned outputs are in Y and in the corresponding allowed sets A(a), A(b) and A(c).
Correctly decides that the ∃y∀x statement is false.
Proves no common y exists, for example by checking y=1,2,3 against the three allowed sets or by showing their intersection is empty.
Explains that f records input-dependent witnesses chosen after x, while the reversed order demands one global y that works for every input.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S31-T@1.marking: Accept any legal function for (i) and any exhaustive proof that the common intersection is empty for (ii). Do not award the final explanation for merely repeating the quantifier symbols.

prerequisiteAudit.source: Published M02 function intuition; restated locally as y=f(x)

main.note: The lesson explicitly teaches quantifier order, dependence and exact negation; Main requires reconstructing those moves on a new integer relation and choosing a legal witness/refuter.

transfer.note: The learner must recast nested quantifiers as a finite assignment/function and common-intersection problem; the exact allowed-set table and successful function are not rehearsed in the lesson.

transfer.decision: Translate allowed-output sets into a dependent function for ∀∃ and into a common-intersection requirement for ∃∀.
transfer.scoredLearnerAction: Constructs a legal f for all three inputs; exhaustively proves no one y lies in all three allowed sets; explains dependent versus global witness semantics.
transfer.classificationJustification: The prompt supplies the finite relation but not the intersection criterion or the successful function. The learner must choose a representation that makes the quantifier order operational.

wrongSolverAudit.wrongApproach: Choose a different y for each x while claiming this proves ∃y∀x, or swap the quantifier symbols without negating the predicate.
wrongSolverAudit.requiredDiscrimination: Main requires one fixed m for the ∃∀ reading and exact nested negation; Transfer requires either one common y or an exhaustive proof none exists.

mathChecks.mainWitness: m=n+1 gives odd difference 1 for every integer n.
mathChecks.mainRefutation: For every proposed integer m in B, n=m is legal and makes m>n false.
